power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: On the size of the model selection problem in a conjoint measurement experiment

text.text: We examine how the number of models respecting marginality in model selection using Maximum Likelihood Conjoint Measurement (MLCM) varies with the number of dimensions tested and explain the logic for determining this number.
The results are related to Dedekind numbers, which increase super-exponentially, and, thus, suggest a limit to the number of dimensions that can be practically tested using the MLCM paradigm.

How organisms integrate features along different sensory dimensions and across modalities is a fundamental problem in perception that is often studied in the context of cue combination (Ernst & Banks, 2002; Oruç, Maloney, & Landy, 2003; Young, Landy, 1 & Maloney, 1993).
text.formatted: How organisms integrate features along different sensory dimensions and across modalities is a fundamental problem in perception that is often studied in the context of cue combination <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Ernst & Banks, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Oruç, Maloney, & Landy, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Young, Landy, 1 & Maloney, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Such experiments often require the subject to match or estimate sensory magnitudes (e.g., Badde, Navarro, & Landy, 2020).
text.formatted: Such experiments often require the subject to match or estimate sensory magnitudes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Badde, Navarro, & Landy, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Maximum Likelihood Conjoint Measurement (MLCM) provides an alternative approach in which observers only make ordinal judgments between stimulus pairs and in which perceptual scales associated with multiple stimulus dimensions can be assessed within a single experiment.

The method has seen extensive use recently in vision experiments that deal with topics as diverse as perception of surface and illuminance properties (Aguilar & Maertens, 2018 , 2022; Chadwick, Cox, Smithson, & Kentridge, 2018; Emrith, Chantler, Green, Maloney, & Clarke, 2010; Hansmann-Roth & Mamassian, 2017 , 2025; Harvey & Smithson, 2021; Ho, Landy, & Maloney, 2008), color perception in adults (Devinck & Knoblauch, 2023 , 2025; Rogers, Knoblauch, & Franklin, 2016; Xie & Fairchild, 2023) and infants (Rogers, Franklin, & Knoblauch, 2018), texture regularity (Sun, St-Amand, Baker Jr, & Kingdom, 2021), blur perception in color vision (Kingdom, Bell, Haddad, & Bartsch, 2015), face perception in aging (Fitousi, 2021), time constancy (Lisi & Gorea, 2016), perception of numeric magnitude (Fitousi, 2022) and multimodal integration (Abbatecola, Gerardin, Beneyton, Kennedy, & Knoblauch, 2021; Abbatecola, Kennedy, & Knoblauch, 2025).
text.formatted: The method has seen extensive use recently in vision experiments that deal with topics as diverse as perception of surface and illuminance properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aguilar & Maertens, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Chadwick, Cox, Smithson, & Kentridge, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Emrith, Chantler, Green, Maloney, & Clarke, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hansmann-Roth & Mamassian, 2017</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Harvey & Smithson, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ho, Landy, & Maloney, 2008)</ref>, color perception in adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Devinck & Knoblauch, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Rogers, Knoblauch, & Franklin, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Xie & Fairchild, 2023)</ref> and infants <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Rogers, Franklin, & Knoblauch, 2018)</ref>, texture regularity <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Sun, St-Amand, Baker Jr, & Kingdom, 2021)</ref>, blur perception in color vision <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kingdom, Bell, Haddad, & Bartsch, 2015)</ref>, face perception in aging <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fitousi, 2021)</ref>, time constancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lisi & Gorea, 2016)</ref>, perception of numeric magnitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fitousi, 2022)</ref> and multimodal integration <ref type="bibr">(Abbatecola, Gerardin, Beneyton, Kennedy, & Knoblauch, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Abbatecola, Kennedy, & Knoblauch, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While estimation of sensory magnitudes is rapid and often generates results in agreement with those based on ordinal judgments (e.g., Devinck & Knoblauch, 2023 , 2025), ordinal judgments are generally easier for subjects to perform, require minimal task demands (Firestone & Scholl, 2016) and constrain underlying perceptual scales with fewer assumptions on the observer's decision processes and on the properties of the underlying scales (Victor, Aguilar, & Waraich, 2025).
text.formatted: While estimation of sensory magnitudes is rapid and often generates results in agreement with those based on ordinal judgments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Devinck & Knoblauch, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2025)</ref>, ordinal judgments are generally easier for subjects to perform, require minimal task demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Firestone & Scholl, 2016)</ref> and constrain underlying perceptual scales with fewer assumptions on the observer's decision processes and on the properties of the underlying scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Victor, Aguilar, & Waraich, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: MLCM is an extension of Conjoint Measurement (CM) that was orignially formulated to demonstrate that continuous scales can be derived from psychological judgments (Luce & Tukey, 1964).
text.formatted: MLCM is an extension of Conjoint Measurement (CM) that was orignially formulated to demonstrate that continuous scales can be derived from psychological judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Luce & Tukey, 1964)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, MLCM extends CM to include a model of error that the original theory was lacking, to facilitate its use empirically.
The psychophysical paradigm involves ordinal comparisons between pairs of stimuli that covary independently along multiple stimulus dimensions.

The underlying perceptual scales and their mutual influences are estimated to maximize the probability of the observer's choices across all experimental trials using a maximum likelihood procedure that incorporates a signal detection model of the observer's decision process (Green & Swets, 1966 /1974).
text.formatted: The underlying perceptual scales and their mutual influences are estimated to maximize the probability of the observer's choices across all experimental trials using a maximum likelihood procedure that incorporates a signal detection model of the observer's decision process <ref type="bibr">(Green & Swets, 1966</ref> <ref type="bibr">/1974)</ref>.

text.text: While the probability model depends on binary choices (paired-comparisons), the set of decision models forms a nested hierarchy equivalent to that obtained in a d-way factorial analysis of variance, including main effects for each dimension and their interactions potentially over multiple orders.
Here, we describe how the number of dimensions manipulated as independent variables determines the number of nested model comparisons available to test.

In our recent article (Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025), we presented an equation for calculating the maximum number of models that might be tested in a d-dimensional comparison in an analysis of data using MLCM that provides correct values for the small models that we analyzed in our paper, i.e., using 2 or 3 stimulus dimensions, but not for models using d > 3 stimulus dimensions.
text.formatted: In our recent article <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025)</ref>, we presented an equation for calculating the maximum number of models that might be tested in a d-dimensional comparison in an analysis of data using MLCM that provides correct values for the small models that we analyzed in our paper, i.e., using 2 or 3 stimulus dimensions, but not for models using d > 3 stimulus dimensions.

text.text: The equation that we gave for the number, N , of possible models respecting marginality conditions is where d is the number of dimensions tested.
For values of d equal to 2 and 3, the equation yields the correct values of 5 and 19, respectively, but not for higher values.
For example, the equation gives the values of 65, 211 and 665 for d = 4, 5 and 6 respectively, whereas the correct values are 167, 7580 and 7828353.

We verified the correct value for d = 4 by brute force using the dredge function from the package MuMIn (Bartoń, 2025) in the openSource software R (R Core Team, 2025) that generates all models respecting marginality for automatic model selection.
text.formatted: We verified the correct value for d = 4 by brute force using the dredge function from the package MuMIn <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bartoń, 2025)</ref> in the openSource software R (R Core Team, 2025) that generates all models respecting marginality for automatic model selection.

text.text: This function only works, however, for models having up to 4 main effects.
To understand the rapid growth of the correct values requires additional explanation.
The question is, given a d-factor experiment, how many nested model sequences can be evaluated (see also Nardi & Rinaldo, 2012, for a discussion of this issue in the context of log-linear models.)?
text.formatted: The question is, given a d-factor experiment, how many nested model sequences can be evaluated (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Nardi & Rinaldo, 2012</ref>, for a discussion of this issue in the context of log-linear models.)?

text.text: Specifically, in nested likelihood ratio testing, a model is evaluated against a similar model with one term from the higher order model removed or set to 0 with all other marginal terms retained (Knoblauch & Maloney, 2012; Wilks, 1938).
text.formatted: Specifically, in nested likelihood ratio testing, a model is evaluated against a similar model with one term from the higher order model removed or set to 0 with all other marginal terms retained <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Knoblauch & Maloney, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wilks, 1938)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the last column of Table 1 lists all possible models respecting marginality for a 2-factor experiment with factors a and b.
text.formatted: For example, the last column of Table <ref type="table">1</ref> lists all possible models respecting marginality for a 2-factor experiment with factors a and b.

text.text: The 4 model terms are indicated in the heading with the 1 indicating an intercept and the term a:b a 2-way interaction.
The significance of the 2-way interaction can be tested against the additive model by comparing the models in rows 5 and 6.
The additive model contains all of the terms in the column heading except the interaction.
Similarly, the additive model can be compared with either of the 1-factor models (row 3 or 4), and each of the 1-factor models with the intercept (row 1).

The model relations might also be depicted in a hierarchical graph or Hasse diagram with the two main effects models (rows 3 and 4) on the same level (Figure 1), illustrating the marginality relations more clearly.
text.formatted: The model relations might also be depicted in a hierarchical graph or Hasse diagram with the two main effects models (rows 3 and 4) on the same level (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), illustrating the marginality relations more clearly.

text.text: An example of a model comparison not respecting marginality would be comparing the model 1 + a + b + a:b with 1 + b + a:b.
The a term marginal to the interaction is missing.
Note that there are 5 such nested models that can be described.
In a 3factor model there would be 19, as we illustrated previously (Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025).
text.formatted: In a 3factor model there would be 19, as we illustrated previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: With so many model comparisons to perform, the issue of conducting multiple hypothesis tests also arises.
We treat that problem elsewhere (Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025).
text.formatted: We treat that problem elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Table 1 Boolean sequences for inclusion/exclusion of terms for all models of a 2-way factorial experiment.
The 0/1 in columns 2-5 indicate the absence/presence of a model term and the Model column indicates the model specification for that row using R formula notation.
All pairs are monotone except rows 3 and 4.
However, these are monotone with the other rows above and below them.
1 a b a:b Model The 0's and 1's in Table 1 are Boolean variables indicating the absence or presence, respectively, of a model term.
text.formatted: 1 a b a:b Model The 0's and 1's in Table <ref type="table">1</ref> are Boolean variables indicating the absence or presence, respectively, of a model term.

text.text: For models to be nested, the columns must follow a monotone Boolean sequence.
This means that within a column, passing from row to row, the sequence can be 0 to 0, 0 to 1 or 1 to 1 but not 1 to 0.
For a pair of models to be nested, all columns must be monotone between the two rows.
Thus, rows 3 and 4 do not form a monotone sequence, but 3 and 5 and 4 and 5 do.
Such sequences are counted by Dedekind numbers (Dedekind, 1897), and they grow super-exponentially with the number of factors.
text.formatted: Such sequences are counted by Dedekind numbers <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dedekind, 1897)</ref>, and they grow super-exponentially with the number of factors.

text.text: Interestingly, the highest Dedekind number computed until now is 9, contains 42 digits and has been determined only recently (Jäkel, 2023; Van Hirtum et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Interestingly, the highest Dedekind number computed until now is 9, contains 42 digits and has been determined only recently <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Jäkel, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Van Hirtum et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The monotone Boolean sequences include the model in which all terms equal 0, row 1, but such a model is only exceptionally of interest in statistical comparisons.
With MLCM, the null model corresponds to the situation for which the probability of a choice is independent of all of the dimensions, i.e., row 2 in Table 1.
text.formatted: With MLCM, the null model corresponds to the situation for which the probability of a choice is independent of all of the dimensions, i.e., row 2 in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the number of models in which we are interested is one less than the Dedekind number or 5 in this case. Kisielewicz (1988) derived the following equation to calculate Dedekind numbers where b k i is the i th bit of the number k in base 2 and the log 2 value of the upper limit of the innermost product is truncated to the nearest integer.
text.formatted: Thus, the number of models in which we are interested is one less than the Dedekind number or 5 in this case. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kisielewicz (1988)</ref> derived the following equation to calculate Dedekind numbers where b k i is the i th bit of the number k in base 2 and the log 2 value of the upper limit of the innermost product is truncated to the nearest integer.

text.text: However, the formula is only useful for calculating low values.

For example, using an inline C++ script embedded in R via the package Rcpp (Eddelbuettel, 2013) (shown in the code below), the formula is accurate for values up to d = 4, afterwhich the upper limit of the summation overflows the size of the default 32-bit integer and yields incorrect values.

text.text: Considering the combinatorial complexity demonstrated here, MLCM experiments have mostly employed just 2 dimensions, but a few have used 3 (Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025; Hansmann-Roth, 2026; Sun et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Considering the combinatorial complexity demonstrated here, MLCM experiments have mostly employed just 2 dimensions, but a few have used 3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Devinck & Knoblauch, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hansmann-Roth, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Sun et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the issues considered above do not affect the overall results or interpretations in our paper.

Given the number of possible models to evaluate, however, it is unlikely that 4 or more dimensions would be attempted (the exception being, perhaps, if there are only a small number of a priori hypotheses of interest), but in the spirit of general understanding and giving pause to researchers planning large MLCM experiments, we thought that it would be of interest and value to describe the logic of the more general solution to this problem.
The full list of known Dedekind numbers is available on the Wikipedia page for Dedekind number (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_number).
